items.title: Headlines for November 05, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Vance Blames Republican Election Losses on the U.S. War on Iran Nov 05, 2026 Democrats are continuing to build on historic gains in U.S. midterm elections, as late returns show Tuesday’s blue wave could rival Democrats’ sweep of the 1974 elections that followed the Watergate scandal. When the 120th Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress for the first time in four years. And this time, they’ll have significantly larger majorities. In the House, Democrats have won at least 240 seats compared to 147 for Republicans, with four dozen races yet to be called. Democrats are projected to surpass 250 seats in the House. In the Senate, the Democratic caucus will grow to at least 54 senators, with two races — Alaska and Mississippi — too close to call. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan by just 637 votes, with nearly a quarter of ballots yet to be counted. Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system means it could take days or weeks to determine the winner. Mississippi’s Senate race remains dramatically close, with the latest numbers showing Democrat Scott Colom ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,100 votes. Colom is now favored to win, as only a few thousand provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots remain to be counted. In a lengthy social media post, Vice President JD Vance blamed historic Republican election losses squarely on the war on Iran. Vance wrote, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” On Wednesday, reporters asked President Trump about Vance’s comments. > Reporter: “Mr. President, Vice President Vance says the reason Republicans lost the war — lost last night was the war in Iran.” > President Donald Trump: “Well, I think it’s largely true, because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term. And probably that’s — probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because, long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” President Trump held his post-election news conference outside the White House ballroom he’s building, signing one of the beams. Iran’s leadership responded to the U.S. election with a warning that any renewed attacks would draw a far wider response. A written statement attributed to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei argued Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility.” ... ## Yemeni Government Claims to Have Thwarted Large-Scale Attack by Ansar Allah in Taiz ... In Yemen, forces loyal to the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government say they’ve fended off a large-scale attack by Ansar Allah fighters in Taiz governate. The violence added to a growing humanitarian crisis in the city of Taiz, where residents are short on water, food, fuel and medical supplies. On Wednesday, the Red Cross said it had delivered four truckloads of essential goods to Taiz. That’s a tiny fraction of what’s needed. The United Nations is urging Yemen’s warring parties to fully reopen roads into Taiz. ... ## World Health Organization Approves Trials of Two New Ebola Vaccines The World Health Organization has approved trials of two new vaccines built specifically for the latest deadly strain of Ebola. The virus has killed more than 5,300 people since May, most of them in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the largest outbreak in the country’s history. The latest strain of Ebola kills about half of those infected. This Meg Doherty, a director at the World Health Organization. > Dr. Meg Doherty: “We’re looking for early results, we hope, in early 2027, so that we can then start to be thinking realistically about that post-trial access and using these vaccines in the countermeasures and really helping to save lives, stop onward infections and help bring the overall epidemic to an end.” ## Paraguay Central Bank Takes Over Lender with Close Ties to President Peña In Paraguay, the central bank took over Ueno Bank, a digital lender with close ties to President Santiago Peña, after its capital fell below half the legal minimum, freezing the accounts of about 3 million customers and hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, including state pension money. Prosecutors have ordered the arrests of eight people, among them the bank’s president and chief executive. Opposition senators are now seeking Peña’s impeachment.

items.title: Top news of the day: November 5, 2026 - The Hindu
items.excerpt: #### ‘Very few complaints’ received so far on police brutality during July 20 protests, says Supreme Court The Supreme Court, on Thursday (November 5, 2026), observed that the High Powered Enquiry Committee (HPEC) looking into police brutality during the July 20 protests reported that “very few complaints” were received. The Action Taken Report issued on October 31 noted that none were received physically or online. The Court allowed petitioners the liberty to forward whatever material they have, including video clips, to the HPEC for its consideration. The apex court said the HPEC has started a new portal through which complaints could be filed anonymously. Petitioners ask why the Delhi Police has not placed on record before HPEC information on the kind of ammunition used on the day. The Court says HPEC may be waiting to collate all details and material before commencing an enquiry. However, the Court said HPEC has to examine material already received and start furnishing fact-finding reports without delay .The court directed the HPEC to submit its first fact-finding report within a month, saying it cannot wait indefinitely for complaints. #### At least two bodies recovered, several feared trapped after building collapses in Old Delhi At least two bodies have been identified and several others are feared trapped after a three-storey building under construction collapsed in Gali Sattara, Sheesh Mahal, near Chawri Bazaar Metro station in Old Delhi on Thursday (November 5, 2026) morning. According to the Delhi Fire Services, a call regarding the building collapse was received at 9.50 a.m.. Four persons were already rescued by locals and shifted to hospital before fire personnel arrived, they said. At least six fire units, including water tenders and rescue vehicles, were rushed to the spot. According to DCP (Central) Rohit Rajbir Singh, around 15 construction workers were present at the site when the building collapsed. Six to seven workers have been accounted for so far, of whom four escaped unhurt. Three workers were pulled out of the debris; two were declared dead, while the third is out of danger.

items.title: Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 7:11 AM EST Updated Thu, Nov 5 2026 9:33 AM EST ... The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did. Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial intelligence tail wind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy. "It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away." Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now. ... "I don't expect any change in economic policy. The Iran war, the tariffs and trade policy, the heavy-handed immigration policy, all are done under executive order. They're not legislatively driven," Zandi said. "The president thought they were good policies before the election. I don't know why he'd change his mind after the election," Zandi added. "So I think they will continue to be policies that restrain growth and add to inflationary pressures and interest rates." Zandi sees the AI hyperscaler buildout as a key to economic growth, but also a source of potential peril. "The risks are decidedly to the downside because the growth is so dependent on AI, and the AI growth effects are so dependent on the equity market, and the equity market is so dependent on the valuations," he said. ... ## Two economies The election happened amid a dichotomy in economic views. Top-line numbers such as gross domestic product, consumer spending and the unemployment rate tell the story of an economy growing briskly while consumers spend and most Americans who want jobs are at work. GDP accelerated at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter while consumer spending grew 3.8%. The unemployment rate is at 4.2% while layoffs are around their lowest level since 1969. However, rising prices have overshadowed those otherwise solid metrics. The inflation rate in September as judged by the consumer price index was 3.7% — up sharply from 2.3% in April 2025 when Trump announced an aggressive round of so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. The Iran war has only aggravated those conditions. The CPI was at just 2.4% when the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, a war that has caused gas prices to soar. And wages aren't keeping up with rising costs. Wage growth when adjusted for inflation has turned negative, down 0.7% from a year ago in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

items.title: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 9:29 AM EST Updated 6 Hours Ago Jeff Cox@jeff.cox.7528@JeffCoxCNBCcom Key Points - Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further - A gradual rate of increases "makes sense," Barkin said. - Inflation "is the most important risk right now," and artificial intelligence is pushing prices up, he said. Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's not sure by how much or at what pace. In a CNBC interview that was part of the Richmond Fed's 2026 CFO Summit, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust. "Unemployment's near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace," Barkin said in the talk with CNBC's Steve Liesman. "Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period. And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me," he added. Barkin's comments come a little more than a week after his colleagues voted to keep the Fed's benchmark overnight borrowing rate anchored in a range between 3.75% and 4%. While Barkin is not a voting member on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee now, he will be in 2027. In its post-meeting statement, the FOMC said it is awaiting the "accumulation of more information" as it deliberates where to go next. When the committee OK'd a quarter percentage point hike in September, officials largely agreed that another increase was likely before the end of 2026. Markets are pricing in a better than 80% chance of a hike in December, then one more move in 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Barkin said he considers current policy close to a point where it neither restricts nor promotes growth, which officials consider a neutral rate. ... "If you're restricting the economy, presumably you're restricting consumption, which is you know roughly two-thirds of the economy, and that's relatively elevated," he said. "So that would make the case that we're a little bit accommodative." Inflation, he added, "is the most important risk right now ... and I hope that our move in September and whatever else we might choose to do in the future will have some impact on inflation." Artificial intelligence is one source of price pressures, though he said it eventually will spur production and help ease inflation further down the road.

items.title: U.S. crude oil rises back above $90 as investors weigh uncertainties around Iran war
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 12:02 AM EST Updated An Hour Ago Oil prices fell for a fourth day on Thursday on expectations the losses U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered in Congressional elections this week may reduce the risk of further escalation of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Todd Korol | Reuters Crude oil prices jumped Thursday, as investors reassessed the outlook for ‌the US-Israeli war with Iran while new attacks on tankers fed worries about oil supplies. Brent Add To Watchlist crude futures rose 3.8% to close at $98.29 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist crude increased 2.7% to settle at $90.52 a barrel. On Wednesday, both benchmarks tumbled more than 8% to their lowest settlement levels since August 31. "The situation in the Middle East is ​still unresolved and that's why there is some modest recovery in prices at the moment," said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at UBS. Andy Lipow, ​president of Lipow Oil Associates, said reports of tankers striking mines in the Middle East or being targeted by drones continue ⁠to worry the oil market. Investors are also worried about Iran's unchanged position regarding negotiations with the US. Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are ​still running close to a record pace with at least five vessels having reported incidents since Sunday, according to UK maritime security agency UKMTO. The pace was ​similar to October when the agency said 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war. The war on Iran, which US President Donald Trump launched along with Israel in February, resulted in sharply higher fuel prices, which became major grievances for voters. Democrats took control of both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, routing Trump's ​Republican Party.

items.excerpt: Lady Gaga, Shakira, Jack White and Boy George lead the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame nominees NEW YORK (AP) — Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Boy George, Jack White, Sia, Vince Gill, Ne-Yo, Blondie’s Debbie Harry and Chris Stein are among the impressive list of nominees for the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame class. Also on the ballot are America’s Gerry Beckley and Dewey Bunnell, Grandmaster Melle Mel as well as members of ZZ Top and War. Eligible voting members have until midnight Eastern Standard Time on Dec. 14 to turn in ballots with their choices of up to three nominees from the songwriter category and up to three from the performing-songwriter category. The 2027 inductees will be announced in early 2027. Last year's class included Taylor Swift, Kiss’s Gene Simmons, Paul Stanley and more. Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault charges on allegations dating back more than 20 years. A judge announced Thursday that Brand would receive a prison sentence. A prosecutor described him as a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator.” Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will. Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and attempted indecent assault. ... NEW YORK (AP) — The new Met Gala exhibit will examine ordinary items and materials like jeans, puffer jackets and plastic and how fashion designers transform them. The new theme announced Thursday sounds about as far as can be imagined from the glittering, elaborate designs of John Galliano. The British designer was originally slated to be the subject of the Met’s fashion exhibit next spring before that idea was scuttled amid an outcry over past antisemitic and racist statements. Costume Institute curator Andrew Bolton tells The Associated Press that it was a scramble to come up with “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” after the cancellation. Everything you need to know about the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards. Here's how to watch NEW YORK (AP) — The 2026 Latin Grammy Awards are back, with the show set for Nov. 12 at Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena. Roselyn Sánchez is hosting for the tenth time. It will be broadcast live on TelevisaUnivision’s U.S. platforms starting at 8 p.m. Eastern, with a pre-show at 7 p.m. Eastern and an apnews.com livestream from the red carpet at 5 p.m. Eastern. Performers include Anitta, Daddy Yankee, Grupo Frontera and many more. A tribute to ranchero icon José Alfredo Jiménez is planned. Producer Edgar Barrera leads the nominations with 10, followed by seven each for Karol G, Rosalía, Jorge Drexler and hip hop duo Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso. ... Movie Review: In 'I Play Rocky,' a middleweight crowd-pleaser about the making of a classic “I Play Rocky,” Peter Farrelly’s fun and featherweight tale about the making of “Rocky,” might seem like a one-two punch of pure nostalgia. It’s been almost exactly 50 years since Sylvester Stallone’s breakthrough boxing classic first arrived in theaters. You need hardly more than a few Philadelphia steps or a holler of “Adrian” to summon its still-ubiquitous cultural presence. But while “I Play Rocky” is far from lacking in memory-lane sentimentality, it’s more aimed at now than it might appear. Today’s movie industry is so corporate and risk-averse that Farrelly’s “Rocky” revival is most enjoyable as a reminder that the movies are a quixotic, even goofy undertaking, writes AP Film Writer Jake Coyle in his review. South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho revisits AI themes in latest thriller 'Paradise Lost' SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho explores artificial intelligence in his films, including his latest, “Paradise Lost.” The psychological thriller follows a mother who spends nine years with an AI version of her missing son until the real one returns. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and opens in North American theaters Friday. Yeon’s inspiration came from a story by his mother, which evolved into the film. He discusses AI's role in relationships and its limits, noting that Asian filmmakers may be more receptive to AI than Hollywood. Yeon believes AI accelerates change in the film industry.
